items.name: iOS
items.why: Native and Flutter apps that talk to the APIs with a device token, never a login screen.

items.name: Android
items.why: Same device-token model. Push arrives through Firebase; purchases arrive through Google Play notifications.

items.name: Web · React
items.why: A React 19 shell over a Laravel API for the internal control plane; public sites are server-rendered.
items.instead_of: Vue. Equivalent; the team already knew React.

items.name: TV · car
items.why: Fire TV, Roku and CarPlay companions: a remote control cannot poll, so they hold a socket.io session.
items.instead_of: Polling over HTTP. Rejected: latency and battery.

items.name: Cloudflare
items.why: DNS and proxy in front of everything. The client learns an edge address, never the origin. Terminates TLS close to the visitor.
items.instead_of: Route 53 alone. Rejected: no proxy, no edge TLS.

items.name: nginx
items.why: Accepts from Cloudflare, adds forwarding headers, hands the request to an Octane worker pool or PHP-FPM. Its request id becomes the trace id.
items.instead_of: Caddy. Fine, but nginx configs are shared with the whole fleet.

items.name: CloudFront
items.why: Only where egress cost proved it: the two buckets that made up most of the storage bill. Roughly a hundred dollars a month saved with no app change.
items.instead_of: CloudFront everywhere. Rejected: most buckets do not move enough bytes.

items.name: Load balancer
items.why: One entry point, strict TLS end to end, and a place to move traffic between machines without a DNS change.
items.instead_of: Public IPs behind Cloudflare, which is today. Being retired.

items.name: PHP 8.4
items.why: Typed properties, enums, readonly classes and attributes. The tracer on this page is built on attributes.

items.name: Laravel 12
items.why: One framework for every API, the panel and the packages. One skeleton, one deploy script, two base images. The long tail of small apps stays cheap to keep alive.
items.instead_of: Node or Go per service. Rejected: a one-person team cannot carry two ecosystems.

items.name: Octane · Swoole
items.why: The app boots once per worker instead of once per request. Used only where traffic asks for it; the quiet apps stay on PHP-FPM, which has no long-lived state to leak.
items.instead_of: FrankenPHP or RoadRunner. Equivalent; Swoole was already proven here.

items.name: Sanctum · JWT
items.why: Device JWTs for mobile clients, Sanctum tokens for panels. Every request is attributable and revocable without anyone seeing a login form.
items.instead_of: Passport. Rejected: OAuth flows the apps do not need.

items.name: Spatie suite
items.why: Permissions, translations, transformers, image handling, Slack alerts. Boring, maintained, documented. Not where I want to be original.
items.instead_of: Hand-rolled. Rejected on maintenance cost.

items.name: libvips · ffmpeg
items.why: Images are resized and optimised on write through libvips; video goes through ffmpeg in a worker. Nothing heavy runs inside a request.
items.instead_of: GD and Imagick. Slower and hungrier at the sizes involved.

items.name: OpenAI · Gemini
items.why: Text and vision behind queued workers. Every provider call is wrapped so a swap is a config change and a class, not a rewrite.
items.instead_of: One provider for everything. Rejected: quality and price differ per task.

items.name: Replicate · fal
items.why: Hosted models for image and video generation, plus self-hosted models on RunPod cog workers where a provider was too slow or too expensive.

items.name: ElevenLabs
items.why: Text to speech for the voice products, chunked and streamed to storage before the device is notified.

items.name: App Store · Google Play
items.why: Server notifications and receipt validation on both stores, normalised into 17 typed subscription events by one shared package.
items.instead_of: Trusting the client. Never.

items.name: Adapty
items.why: Paywalls, experiments and store reconciliation without building them. The purchase package keeps native store notifications so the vendor stays replaceable.
items.instead_of: RevenueCat. Equivalent; Adapty was already in the apps.

items.name: Firebase FCM
items.why: Push for every app through one notification package with a driver switch, migrated from another provider without rewriting notification classes.
items.instead_of: Staying on the old provider. Rejected on cost and lock-in.

items.name: MySQL 8
items.why: Per-app databases keep the blast radius small and let the control plane attach to each one. On EC2 today for cost; managed Multi-AZ is the next step once data is separated from compute.
items.instead_of: PostgreSQL. Fine; MySQL is what the fleet already runs.

items.name: Redis
items.why: One shared instance on the data server so app servers can be replaced without touching state. Rate limits, cache and the hot apps' queues live here.
items.instead_of: Memcached. Rejected: no persistence, no queues.

items.name: ClickHouse
items.why: A read-only mirror built for aggregates. Dashboard queries went from thirty seconds on MySQL to well under one.
items.instead_of: MySQL read replicas. Rejected: same engine, same slow aggregates.

items.name: PeerDB
items.why: Streams MySQL binlogs into ClickHouse, seconds behind, so production never runs an analytics query.
items.instead_of: Nightly dumps. Rejected: a day stale and heavy on the source.

items.name: MinIO
items.why: S3-compatible object storage on the data server, used as the landing zone between PeerDB and ClickHouse.

items.name: S3
items.why: Every upload and every generated asset. Public reads go through CloudFront where the bill asked for it.

items.name: AWS EC2 · Graviton
items.why: ARM instances by default: cheaper for the same work, and every image builds for arm64. Sizes come from thirty-day graphs, not habit.
items.instead_of: x86. Kept only where a dependency demanded it; so far nothing has.

items.name: ECS · ECR
items.why: Scale the app, not the server. A task has a memory limit, an out-of-memory kills the task and not the neighbours, an image is an immutable deploy.
items.instead_of: Fargate. Rejected at this profile: 20 to 60 percent premium over the EC2 launch type.

items.name: Docker
items.why: Two base images cover the fleet: PHP-FPM and Octane. Vendor is baked in at build so private packages need no credentials at runtime.

items.name: GitLab CI · Envoy
items.why: Release folders and a current symlink, shared .env and storage, manual production jobs from main. Every app deploys the same way, from inside the network.
items.instead_of: GitHub Actions. Rejected: repos, runners and secrets stay inside.

items.name: Supervisor · PM2
items.why: Supervisor keeps queue workers and schedulers alive for PHP; PM2 does the same for the Node socket services.
items.instead_of: systemd units per app. More ceremony for the same result.

items.name: WireGuard
items.why: A Laravel API leases peers on a fleet of nodes and enforces those leases against payment events on a schedule.
items.instead_of: OpenVPN. Rejected: heavier, slower to provision.

items.name: Nightwatch
items.why: Exceptions, slow routes, slow jobs and scheduled tasks per app. It is how a silent failure in the push package was found.

items.name: Sentry
items.why: Kept where it already was. Nightwatch covers new work.

items.name: Telescope
items.why: Enabled by default it records every scheduled task run in production. Every production .env pins it off.

items.name: Zabbix
items.why: CPU, memory and disk on every EC2 with alerts to Slack. The graphs that decide instance sizes come from here.
items.instead_of: CloudWatch alarms. Not configured yet; on the list.

items.name: Slack alerts
items.why: Apps post their own alerts: failed jobs, provider errors, unusual purchase events.

items.name: Telegram
items.why: A second channel for the alerts that must wake someone up.
